title: Indian-American Voters Show Highest Enthusiasm Among Asian Americans Ahead of 2026 Midterms
excerpt: The 2026 AAPI Voter Survey finds 92% of Indian-American registered voters plan to vote in November, with 66% backing Democratic candidates for Congress.
body:
• 92% of Indian-American registered voters plan to vote in the November 2026 midterm elections, according to the 2026 AAPI Voter Survey released by APIAVote and AAPI Data.
  • Indian Americans record the highest increase in voting enthusiasm among all major Asian ethnic groups, with 43% saying they are more enthusiastic than usual.
  • 66% of Indian-American voters support Democratic candidates in both Senate and House races, compared with 22% and 18% for Republicans respectively.
  • 42% of AAPI voters report no contact from the Democratic Party and 58% no contact from Republicans, signaling untapped outreach potential.

Indian-American voters are emerging as one of the most politically engaged communities in the United States ahead of the November midterm elections, according to the 2026 Asian American Voter Survey released by APIAVote and AAPI Data on August 26.

The survey, which has tracked the attitudes and voting behavior of Asian American and Pacific Islander (AAPI) voters since 2012, found that 92% of Indian-American registered voters plan to cast ballots in the 2026 midterms. Of those, 74% said they were absolutely certain they would vote, while another 23% were fairly certain.

Highest Enthusiasm Among Asian Americans

Indian Americans recorded the sharpest increase in voting enthusiasm among all major Asian ethnic groups surveyed. Forty-three percent said they were more enthusiastic about voting than in previous elections, compared with 22% who were less enthusiastic and 32% who reported about the same level of interest.

The broader AAPI community also showed strong engagement: 90% of registered AAPI voters overall said they plan to vote in November, up from 84% in 2022 and 86% in 2018. There are now an estimated 16 million eligible AAPI voters nationwide, an increase of 1.6 million since 2022.

"With Asian Americans being the fastest-growing electorate in the country, it's crucial that we have the latest data on what motivates them to turn out and vote."

— Karthick Ramakrishnan, Founder and Executive Director, AAPI Data

Strong Democratic Lean in Congressional Races

The survey revealed a pronounced preference for Democratic candidates among Indian-American voters. In Senate races, 66% supported Democratic candidates while 22% favored Republicans and 7% preferred another party. The pattern held in House races, where 66% backed Democrats compared with 18% for Republicans and 9% for other parties.

Among Indian Americans expressing a House preference, 60% said they strongly supported their chosen candidate, suggesting firm rather than tentative partisan alignment.

Indian Americans showed the strongest Democratic preference among all Asian American subgroups surveyed. Support for Democratic Senate candidates ranged from a low of 42% among Filipino voters — the only group where Republican preference (49%) exceeded Democratic — to 66% among Indian Americans.

Views on Trump and Key Issues

The survey found largely negative views of President Donald Trump among Indian-American voters. Seventy-four percent viewed Trump unfavorably, including 56% who held a very unfavorable opinion. Twenty percent viewed him favorably, with 7% holding a very favorable view.

Across the broader AAPI community, cost of living and inflation dominated voter concerns, with 90% of Asian Americans and 89% of Pacific Islanders calling it very or extremely important in deciding how they vote. On this top issue, 44% of AAPI voters trusted Democrats to do a better job compared with 18% who trusted Republicans.

Parties Leaving Voters Unreached

Despite the community's growing electoral weight, a significant portion of AAPI voters reported no contact from either major party. Forty-two percent said they had not been reached by the Democratic Party, while 58% reported no contact from Republicans.

Community organizations reached roughly as many AAPI adults as the Democratic Party, with 58% reporting some contact from each. Family and friends (62%) and academic experts (60%) ranked as the most trusted messengers on political issues, followed by community journalists (50%) and AAPI-serving organizations (47%).

"This year we are seeing even more voters planning to cast their ballots for the midterms."

— Christine Chen, Founder and Executive Director, APIAVote

Three-quarters of Indian Americans reported discussing politics with family or friends over the past year. Nineteen percent had participated in protests, marches, or rallies, while 20% attended local government meetings such as city council or school board sessions — reflecting civic engagement that extends well beyond the ballot box.

Indian Americans were also more likely than other major Asian-American groups to prefer in-person voting, with 55% planning to vote at polling locations, 34% opting for mail-in ballots, and 8% intending to use ballot drop-off sites.
